subsection: 1. The Home Rule movement: origins, Butt and the rise of Parnell, 1870–1885

notes.h: Background: why Home Rule emerged around 1870
notes.b: By 1870 Irish nationalism had tried repeal, rebellion and Fenian conspiracy without success. Home Rule offered a constitutional, moderate alternative that might attract Protestants as well as Catholics.
points: The Act of Union (in force from 1 January 1801) abolished the Irish parliament, so Irish MPs sat at Westminster and decisions on Irish affairs were made there.
Daniel O’Connell’s Repeal campaign (the demand to undo the Union) peaked in 1843 but failed in the 1840s, and the Young Ireland rising of 1848 collapsed.

The Fenians (the IRB, the Irish Republican Brotherhood) wanted an Irish republic won by force. Their rising of 1867 was crushed, but the arrest and trial of Fenians produced a public movement in 1869 for an amnesty (a pardon) for political prisoners, and Isaac Butt took part in it.
Clan na Gael was the Irish-American Fenian organisation, so it later became an important source of money and support for Irish nationalists.

Gladstone became Prime Minister in December 1868 saying his mission was to pacify Ireland. He passed the Irish Church Act (1869), disestablishing the Church of Ireland (ending its status as the state church, from 1871), and a first Land Act in 1870.
Those reforms did not satisfy nationalists, because the 1870 Land Act gave tenants compensation for improvements and for disturbance but no secure tenure or fair rents, so tenants stayed insecure.

In the 1860s Irish MPs were mostly Liberals or Conservatives rather than members of a separate Irish party, so nobody pressed for self-government in a united way. This gap is what the Home Rule movement set out to fill.
notes.tip: Exams ask why Home Rule emerged. Give the failure of repeal, rebellion and Fenianism, the amnesty movement, disappointment with Gladstone’s reforms, and the hope of a constitutional alternative that might include Protestants.

notes.h: Key concepts: Home Rule, democracy and political agitation
notes.b: Three ideas run through this whole topic. Knowing exactly what each means as used here stops you mixing Butt’s moderate aims with Fenian separatism.
points: Home Rule meant an Irish parliament for domestic affairs within the United Kingdom and empire. It was not separation, which is why it differed from the Fenian demand for a republic and could appeal to moderates and Protestants.

Democracy here means government by elected representatives answerable to voters. In this period it showed itself in the secret ballot, in a disciplined party that spoke for its voters, and in the widening of the voters’ influence.

Political agitation means organised public pressure through meetings, newspapers, petitions, elections and parliamentary tactics, rather than violence. O’Connell had used it to build a mass base, and Home Rulers hoped to do the same.
notes.tip: Be ready to define Home Rule as a parliament for domestic affairs inside the United Kingdom and empire, not independence. Mixing it up with the Fenian republic is a common mistake.

notes.h: Isaac Butt and his federal idea
notes.b: Isaac Butt, a Protestant barrister and former Conservative MP, founded the movement in Dublin in 1870. His own journey from unionism to nationalism shows why Home Rule could appeal to people who rejected the Fenians.
points: Butt (1813–1879) was born in Co. Donegal, the son of a Church of Ireland clergyman. He became a Dublin barrister, professor of political economy at Trinity College Dublin, and a Conservative MP in the 1850s and 1860s.

He began as a unionist opponent of O’Connell, but defending the Young Irelanders in 1848 and Fenian prisoners in the 1860s turned him towards nationalism. He also took part in the 1869 amnesty campaign.

Butt’s programme was federal: a parliament in Dublin would deal with domestic affairs, while Westminster kept control of the empire, defence and foreign policy. This kept Ireland inside the empire, which made the plan acceptable to moderates.
Butt’s method was constitutional: persuasion, parliamentary motions and public meetings, and a rejection of physical force, so he could appeal to people who would never back the Fenians.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph on Butt, give his background (Donegal-born Protestant, Dublin barrister, former Conservative), then federal Home Rule. Each correct fact earns a mark.

notes.h: The Home Government Association, Limerick, the Ballot Act and the Home Rule League (1870–1873)
notes.b: Butt turned an idea into an organisation in three steps: an association, a by-election win and a parliamentary party. The Ballot Act helped by making it safer for voters to back him.
points: The Home Government Association was founded in Dublin in May 1870. Its members included Conservatives, Liberals, former Repealers and Catholic moderates, so it was a deliberately cross-party body.
Butt won the Limerick City by-election in 1871 as a Home Ruler, which showed that the new demand could win votes.
The Ballot Act (1872) introduced the secret ballot, so landlords and agents could no longer watch how tenants voted. This reduced landlord pressure on voters.
The Galway election petition of 1872 heard evidence of priests pressing voters, so clerical pressure was also a concern.
A national conference in Dublin in November 1873 replaced the Association with the Home Rule League. Its MPs were to form a distinct, independent party pledged to act together.

Remember the three similar names, because they are easily confused: the Association (1870) was the first body, and the League (1873) was the party. The Home Rule Confederation of Great Britain was a separate body that organised Irish voters in England.
notes.tip: Examiners like dated chronology: 1870 Association, 1873 League, 1874 election. Do not confuse the Association, the League and the Confederation of Great Britain.

notes.h: The 1874 election and why Butt’s leadership failed
notes.b: The 1874 election produced the first sizeable Home Rule party, but Butt could not make it effective. His failure explains why more aggressive tactics followed.
points: In the 1874 general election about 60 of the 103 Irish seats were won by Home Rulers (59 or 60 by different counts). They were the first sizeable Home Rule party, though Disraeli’s Conservatives won the election and governed to 1880.

Many of those MPs were Liberals who had taken the Home Rule label for local reasons and did not vote consistently with the party. The League had no pledge or whip to bind them, which meant weak discipline and mixed loyalties.
Butt’s Home Rule motions at Westminster were heavily defeated, and neither Disraeli’s Conservatives nor the Liberals took them seriously.
Butt relied on persuasion, hoping to win English sympathy through argument, but the Commons treated Irish business as a nuisance rather than a priority.

The electorate was small (it was widened only in 1884), and the League had little money or local organisation. The movement therefore remained a body of MPs and lawyers with few roots among tenant farmers.
Younger members, including Joseph Biggar and John O’Connor Power (MP for Mayo from 1874 and an IRB member), believed politeness had failed and demanded a more aggressive policy.

Butt’s health and finances weakened his authority, as he was often in debt. William Shaw succeeded him as party leader in 1879, and Butt died on 5 May 1879, by which time leadership had passed in practice to the obstructionists.
notes.tip: Questions ask why Butt failed. Give several causes: no discipline, mixed loyalties, heavily defeated motions, reliance on persuasion, no money or organisation, impatient rivals, ill health and debt. Do not give a vote count for his defeated motions.

notes.b: Obstruction was the first tactic that forced the House of Commons to take Irish MPs seriously. It showed that a few determined members could use the rules of the House against the government.
points: Obstruction meant prolonged speeches, endless amendments and procedural objections designed to jam Commons business until the government gave way.
Joseph Biggar (1828–1890) began obstruction in 1874–75. He was a Belfast-born Presbyterian provision merchant, a member of the IRB, and MP for Cavan from 1874.
Charles Stewart Parnell was elected MP for Meath in a by-election in April 1875. He joined obstruction in earnest from 1877, and the South Africa Bill debate of 1877 is an early example.
Parnell also broke with Butt’s caution by refusing, in the Commons, to call the executions of the Manchester Martyrs (Fenians executed in November 1867) murder. This won him Fenian respect.
In August 1877 Parnell replaced Butt as president of the Home Rule Confederation of Great Britain, the body that organised Irish voters in English cities.

In January–February 1881 Irish MPs obstructed the coercion bill in a sitting of about 41 hours (31 January–2 February). The Speaker, Henry Brand, ended the debate on his own authority, and the Commons adopted the closure rule (a way to end debate) in 1882.

Both main parties condemned obstruction as an abuse of parliament, and Butt himself deplored it. It still showed that a small, disciplined group could make the House unworkable, which is why the rules were changed.
notes.tip: Obstruction began with Biggar in 1874–75; Parnell joined in earnest from 1877. Do not say Parnell started it. Be able to say what it was and why it worked.

notes.b: The New Departure linked three forces that had worked apart: Fenian-minded nationalists, constitutional Home Rulers and the land-reform movement. Hard times in the countryside made the link possible.
points: The agricultural depression from 1877 (poor harvests, falling prices and cheap American grain imports) brought a threat of evictions and a crisis in the countryside.

Michael Davitt was a Fenian sentenced in 1870 to fifteen years for arms trafficking. Released on licence in December 1877 after about seven years, he travelled to the USA in 1878 and met John Devoy of Clan na Gael.
In October 1878 Devoy telegraphed Parnell, offering Clan na Gael support if he adopted a more active programme: self-government, peasant ownership of land, and an independent parliamentary party.
Parnell never formally accepted the offer, but he moved towards it, so his public alliance with Davitt created the working partnership known as the New Departure.
The New Departure committed Fenians to co-operate with a parliamentary party. This was a break with the IRB’s refusal to accept constitutional politics.
It also tied Home Rule to the land question, so a tenant-farmer movement could supply the votes and funds for national politics.
The alliance was always uneasy. The IRB Supreme Council opposed co-operation, and Davitt favoured land nationalisation while Parnell favoured peasant proprietorship (tenants owning their farms).
notes.tip: Short questions ask what the New Departure was and who made it. Name Devoy, Davitt and Parnell, and say it joined Fenians, land agitation and constitutional politics.

notes.h: Parnell takes the lead: Land League, America and the party chair (1879–1880)
notes.b: Between 1879 and 1880 Parnell turned a land protest into a national organisation and then took control of the parliamentary party.
points: The Irishtown meeting in Co. Mayo (20 April 1879) began the protest. The Land League of Mayo followed in August 1879 and was extended into the Irish National Land League, founded in Dublin in October 1879 with Parnell as president and Davitt a leading organiser.

Parnell and John Dillon toured the United States from January to March 1880, and Parnell addressed the US House of Representatives in February. The tour gave the movement American money and publicity.
At the April 1880 general election about 60 Home Rulers were returned. Parnell was elected for Meath, Mayo and Cork City and chose Cork City, which he held until his death in 1891.

In May 1880 Parnell was elected chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party (the Home Rule MPs), defeating William Shaw by 23 votes to 18. Shaw had been Butt’s successor in 1879, so this transferred leadership to Parnell.
Do not confuse the offices: Parnell was president of the Land League from 1879 and chairman of the party from May 1880.
notes.tip: Keep similar dates straight: Irishtown (April 1879), Land League of Mayo (August 1879), Irish National Land League (October 1879), chairman (May 1880).

notes.h: Kilmainham: coercion, imprisonment and the understanding of 1882
notes.b: Between October 1881 and May 1882 Parnell went from prison to a deal with the government. Its results show how he steered the Land War back into politics.
points: Gladstone’s Chief Secretary, W.E. Forster, introduced coercion in 1881, allowing detention without trial. The Land Act of August 1881 followed.

Parnell was arrested on 13 October 1881 and held in Kilmainham Gaol. From prison he and other leaders issued the No Rent Manifesto, calling on tenants to withhold rent, so the Land League was suppressed within days.
Captain William O’Shea carried messages between Parnell and the government. In April–May 1882 an arrangement was reached, nicknamed the Kilmainham treaty, and Parnell was released on 2 May 1882.

It was an unwritten understanding, not a treaty, because nothing was signed. Parnell signalled that he would help restore order and co-operate with the Liberals, and the government would deal with rent arrears.
Forster resigned in protest at the release, and the Arrears Act (August 1882) cancelled arrears for poorer tenants.

Opinion divides on it. Some read it as a sensible deal that brought land reform and steered Parnell towards parliamentary politics. Critics read it as an opportunistic retreat from the Land League’s aims.
notes.tip: If asked what happened at Kilmainham, give arrest, the No Rent Manifesto, O’Shea, release and the Arrears Act, and say it was an unwritten understanding, not a treaty.

notes.b: Days after Parnell’s release, murders in Dublin threatened to destroy the understanding and to discredit him.
points: On 6 May 1882 Lord Frederick Cavendish, the new Chief Secretary who had arrived in Dublin that day, and Thomas Henry Burke, the Under-Secretary, were stabbed to death in Phoenix Park. Forster, the previous Chief Secretary, had resigned and was not a victim.
The killers were the Invincibles, a small IRB breakaway group (an IRB splinter), who carried out the killings.
Parnell denounced the murders and offered to resign his seat, and Gladstone refused the offer. The government nevertheless introduced the Prevention of Crimes Act (1882).
The informer James Carey gave evidence against his fellow Invincibles, and five of them were hanged in 1883.
notes.tip: Questions ask why the Phoenix Park murders harmed Parnell. Build the answer from what happened: the murders, Parnell’s denunciation and offer to resign, and the Prevention of Crimes Act. Do not mix up Cavendish and Burke (killed) with Forster (resigned).

notes.h: The National League and the party machine (1881–1885)
notes.b: After the Land League was suppressed, Parnell built an organisation he could control. By 1885 it had a press, pledged MPs, a parish network and steady funds.
points: United Ireland, founded in 1881 and edited by William O’Brien, became the party’s weekly newspaper.

The Irish National League, founded in October 1882, replaced the suppressed Land League. It put Home Rule first, with land reform and local self-government, and Parnell kept personal control of it. Do not confuse it with the Land League or with the Irish Parliamentary Party, which was the MPs.

Parish branches of the National League gave the movement an organisation in nearly every county, with priests often serving as chairs or treasurers. This gave Home Rule the local roots Butt had lacked.
By 1884–85 candidates had to take a pledge to sit, act and vote with the party. They were chosen by constituency conventions, with priests prominent, which ended the independent Home Rule MP.
Funding came from the Irish diaspora (Irish emigrants and their descendants, especially in America) and from local collections.
The Parnell Tribute of 1883, a national collection, raised about £37,000 for Parnell, although the Vatican disapproved of it.
By 1885 the result was a mass movement and a disciplined party that was likely to hold the balance of power at Westminster. The election of 1885 would test this.
notes.tip: Be able to say what the pledge did: it bound MPs to act together, so Home Rule MPs could no longer vote as individuals. Pair it with conventions, press and funding as the machine.

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Stewart Parnell (part 1: background and rise)
notes.b: Parnell’s early career shows an unlikely rebel becoming the leader of a mass movement. This part runs from his background to the eve of the 1885 election.
points: Parnell was born in 1846 at Avondale, Co. Wicklow, into a Protestant landowning family; he was not Catholic. His mother, Delia Stewart, was the daughter of an American naval officer.
He studied at Magdalene College, Cambridge, and was High Sheriff of Wicklow in 1874, hardly an obvious future rebel.

His main steps were: elected for Meath in 1875, obstruction with Biggar, the Confederation of Great Britain in 1877, the Land League in 1879, the party chair in 1880, Kilmainham in 1881–82, the National League in 1882 and the pledge in 1884–85.
He was a direct participant. He organised the party, led the Land League, and negotiated with Davitt, Devoy and Gladstone’s government.
He was also shaped by events, for example the agricultural depression, Fenian and American pressure, coercion, imprisonment and the Phoenix Park murders each pushed him in new directions.
His speeches urged tenants to keep a firm grip of their homesteads (Westport, June 1879) and to isolate anyone who took a farm from which a tenant had been evicted (Ennis, September 1880).
In Cork in 1885 he declared that "no man has a right to fix the boundary to the march of a nation".

Supporters admired his aloof, disciplined manner and his ability to hold Fenians and constitutionalists together. Critics, including The Times, unionists, the Vatican (over the Tribute) and some moderates in his own party, distrusted him.
F.S.L. Lyons, in Charles Stewart Parnell (1977), stresses his political skill and the fragile alliance he led. Other historians stress a pragmatic parliamentarian steering the Land War into politics.
notes.tip: Part (d) of a documents question rewards Parnell’s strengths and weaknesses with evidence: organisation, tactics and uniting Fenians, land and parliament, against dependence on alliances and personal control.

notes.b: Judgement turns on whether the movement’s success owed more to Butt’s foundation or to Parnell’s machine. A good answer gives credit and limits to each.
points: Butt’s achievements: he founded a national, respectable and constitutional movement and won about 60 seats in 1874. His limits were that he had no discipline, money or mass base, and won no concession.

Parnell’s achievements: he gave the party discipline (the pledge, conventions), a press, American money and a mass base through the land movement, and by 1885 held the likely balance of power. His limits were dependence on the land movement and on Fenian allies he could not fully control.
Parnell’s structure also rested on his personal control rather than a lasting system, and Home Rule had still not been won.
On land, Butt supported tenant right, but Parnell made land the engine of the national movement, because tenant votes and funds gave it a mass base.
On method, Butt tried to persuade English opinion by argument, whereas Parnell used disruption and organisation.
On social base, Butt’s was gentlemen and lawyers, whereas Parnell’s was a parish-based mass movement. Both were Protestants.
Contemporaries saw Butt as an honourable failure and Parnell as dangerous but effective, because Parnell’s tactics actually won attention.
The overall judgement is that Butt prepared the ground and Parnell built the machine, so the movement needed both.
notes.tip: A strong essay states its thesis at the start, for example that Parnell was more effective because of the pledge, conventions, press and mass base. It then pairs dated evidence for each leader and gives Butt credit rather than dismissing him.

keyTerms.definition: The demand for a parliament in Dublin to manage Ireland’s domestic affairs, with Westminster keeping control of the empire, defence and foreign policy.
Government by the people through elected representatives; in this period it meant widening the franchise and protecting voters through the secret ballot.
Organised public pressure for change using meetings, newspapers, petitions, boycotts and parliamentary tactics rather than violence.
The body founded by Isaac Butt in Dublin in 1870 to campaign for federal Home Rule by constitutional means.
The organisation founded in November 1873 to replace the Association and bind Home Rule MPs into an independent parliamentary party.
A parliamentary tactic of prolonged speeches and amendments used to stop Commons business until the government gave way.
The 1878–79 working alliance of Davitt, Devoy and Parnell linking Fenians, land reformers and constitutional nationalists.
The party of Irish Home Rule MPs, led by Parnell from 1880 and bound by a pledge to act together.
The unwritten 1882 understanding between Parnell and Gladstone under which Parnell was released and the arrears question was addressed.
The organisation founded in October 1882 that succeeded the Land League and became Parnell’s national party machine.
Butt’s model of Home Rule, in which Ireland would have its own parliament for domestic matters while remaining within the United Kingdom and empire.
